prefix_hints.hint_5: Project `AVG(total_amount_purchased)` and `AVG(total_value_purchased)` to return the two requested averages.

Question:

answer: SELECT T1.name_first ,  T1.name_last ,  T2.player_id FROM player AS T1 JOIN manager_award AS T2 ON T1.player_id  =  T2.player_id GROUP BY T2.player_id ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1;

prefix_hints.hint_1: Use the manager-award records to count how many awards each person has won.

prefix_hints.hint_3: Group the joined rows by `manager_award.player_id` to create one result group per manager.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Rank those groups by award count with `ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC`, then retain the top group using `LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the winning manager’s `name_first`, `name_last`, and `player_id` in the requested order.

Question:
In 2014, what are the id and rank of the team that has the largest average number of attendance?
answer: SELECT T2.team_id ,  T2.rank FROM home_game AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id  =  T2.team_id WHERE T1.year  =  2014 GROUP BY T1.team_id ORDER BY avg(T1.attendance) DESC LIMIT 1;

prefix_hints.hint_1: Use `home_game` for attendance records and `team` for the corresponding team rank.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join the tables by matching their team identifiers: `home_game.team_id = team.team_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the attendance records to 2014 with `WHERE home_game.year = 2014`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Group the matched rows by `home_game.team_id`, then rank the groups using `ORDER BY AVG(home_game.attendance) DESC`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Keep only the first ordered group with `LIMIT 1`, and project the team identifier together with its `rank` from `team`.

Question:
What are the first name, last name and id of the player with the most all star game experiences? Also list the count.
answer: SELECT T1.name_first , T1.name_last ,  T1.player_id ,   count(*) FROM player AS T1 JOIN all_star AS T2 ON T1.player_id  =  T2.player_id GROUP BY T1.player_id ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1;

prefix_hints.hint_1: Use the all-star participation records to measure each player's experience, counting each matching row as one all-star game experience.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join player details to those records with `player.player_id = all_star.player_id` so the result can include the player's name and ID.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Group the joined rows by the player's ID, allowing `COUNT(*)` to calculate the number of all-star experiences for each player.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Rank the grouped players by `COUNT(*) DESC` and apply `LIMIT 1` to retain the player with the highest count.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the player's `name_first`, `name_last`, and `player_id` together with `COUNT(*)` as the requested experience count.

Question:

answer: SELECT T1.id ,  T1.name ,  T1.gender FROM architect AS T1 JOIN bridge AS T2 ON T1.id  =  T2.architect_id GROUP BY T1.id HAVING count(*)  =  2 UNION SELECT T1.id ,  T1.name ,  T1.gender FROM architect AS T1 JOIN mill AS T2 ON T1.id  =  T2.architect_id GROUP BY T1.id HAVING count(*)  =  1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Treat the two qualifying conditions as separate result sets: architects associated with exactly two bridges, and architects associated with exactly one mill.
prefix_hints.hint_2: For the bridge branch, join `architect` to `bridge` using `architect.id = bridge.architect_id`, then group the joined rows by the architect ID.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the grouped bridge results with `HAVING COUNT(*) = 2` so each returned architect has exactly two matching bridges.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Build the mill branch similarly by joining on `architect.id = mill.architect_id`, grouping by architect ID, and applying `HAVING COUNT(*) = 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the architect's `id`, `name`, and `gender` in both branches, then combine the two compatible result sets with `UNION`.

prefix_hints.hint_4: Sort the grouped results by `AVG(T1.stars)` in ascending order so the movie with the lowest average appears first.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Select the movie title and its average star rating, then apply `LIMIT 1` to return the first result from that ordering.

prefix_hints.hint_4: Group the joined rows by `DEPARTMENT.SCHOOL_CODE` so that each school forms one aggregation group.

Question:
Find the movies with the highest average rating. Return the movie titles and average rating.
answer: SELECT T2.title ,  avg(T1.stars) FROM Rating AS T1 JOIN Movie AS T2 ON T1.mID  =  T2.mID GROUP BY T1.mID ORDER BY avg(T1.stars) DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Use the rating records to calculate a separate average of `stars` for each movie.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join `Rating` to `Movie` using their shared movie identifier: `T1.mID = T2.mID`, so each average can be paired with its title.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Group the joined rows by `T1.mID` and compute each movie’s score with `AVG(T1.stars)`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Sort the grouped results by `AVG(T1.stars) DESC` so the highest-rated movie appears first.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Select the movie title and its computed average rating, then apply `LIMIT 1` to return the top result.

prefix_hints.hint_2: Build the first set by joining `Student` to `Voting_record` so that the student's `StuID` matches `Voting_record.President_Vote`, identifying the students selected for president.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Project `Student.LName` from this join and apply `DISTINCT` so each qualifying last name appears once.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Build the second set from `Student` by filtering with `Advisor = '8741'` and selecting distinct `LName` values.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Combine the two last-name result sets with `INTERSECT` so the output contains only distinct last names appearing in both sets.

prefix_hints.hint_2: Combine customer details with purchase records by joining `customers` to `invoices`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Use the relationship `invoices.customer_id = customers.id` as the join condition.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Sort the joined rows by `invoice_date` in descending order so the newest purchases appear first, then apply `LIMIT 5`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project only the customer's `first_name` and `last_name` from the five resulting rows.

prefix_hints.hint_4: Filter the grouped results with `HAVING COUNT(...) > 10` to retain albums containing more than ten tracks.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the album `title` from the qualifying groups to produce the requested list.

Question:
Find the subject ID, name of subject and the corresponding number of courses for each subject, and sort by the course count in ascending order.
answer: SELECT T1.subject_id ,  T2.subject_name ,  COUNT(*) FROM Courses AS T1 JOIN Subjects AS T2 ON T1.subject_id  =  T2.subject_id GROUP BY T1.subject_id ORDER BY COUNT(*) ASC

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the course records, since each row represents a course that contributes to a subject’s course count.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join the subject details using `Courses.subject_id = Subjects.subject_id` so each course is paired with its subject name.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Group the joined rows by `Courses.subject_id` to create one result group for each subject.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Use `COUNT(*)` to calculate the number of course rows in every subject group.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the subject ID, subject name, and computed count, then sort the groups with `ORDER BY COUNT(*) ASC`.

Question:
What are the name and id of the team offering the lowest average salary?
answer: SELECT T1.name ,  T1.team_id FROM team AS T1 JOIN salary AS T2 ON T1.team_id = T2.team_id GROUP BY T1.team_id ORDER BY avg(T2.salary) ASC LIMIT 1;

prefix_hints.hint_1: Use salary records to calculate each team's average salary, and use team records to retrieve the corresponding team name and identifier.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join `team` to `salary` using the shared key `team.team_id = salary.team_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Group the joined rows by `team.team_id` so that `AVG(salary.salary)` is computed separately for each team.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Sort the grouped teams by `AVG(salary.salary)` in ascending order and apply `LIMIT 1` to retain the team with the lowest average.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the selected team's `name` and `team_id` from the team table in the final result.

prefix_hints.hint_2: Connect each customer to their loans by joining `customer` and `loan` on the shared `cust_ID` value.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Group the joined rows by `T1.cust_name` so that all loans belonging to the same customer form one group.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Rank the customer groups by their aggregate loan amount using `ORDER BY SUM(T2.amount) DESC`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Select `T1.cust_name` and apply `LIMIT 1` to return the customer at the top of that descending ranking.

prefix_hints.hint_4: Restrict the joined rows to delivered orders with `WHERE t2.order_status = 'Delivered'`.

prefix_hints.hint_4: Restrict the joined rows to the requested club with `WHERE T2.name = 'Boston Red Stockings'`.

Question:
Find the names of rooms that have been reserved for more than 60 times.
answer: SELECT T2.roomName FROM Reservations AS T1 JOIN Rooms AS T2 ON T1.Room  =  T2.RoomId GROUP BY T1.Room HAVING count(*)  >  60

prefix_hints.hint_5: Project `T2.roomName` from the joined room record to return the names of the qualifying rooms.

Question:
What is the total home game attendance of team Boston Red Stockings from 2000 to 2010?
answer: SELECT sum(T1.attendance) FROM home_game AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id  =  T2.team_id_br WHERE T2.name  =  'Boston Red Stockings' AND T1.year BETWEEN 2000 AND 2010;

prefix_hints.hint_1: Use `home_game` as the source of attendance records and `team` to identify the records belonging to the named team.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join the tables using the identifier mapping `home_game.team_id = team.team_id_br`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the joined rows to Boston Red Stockings with `team.name = 'Boston Red Stockings'`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Apply the inclusive year range using `home_game.year BETWEEN 2000 AND 2010`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Return the total by applying `SUM` to the matched `home_game.attendance` values.

Question:
Find Alice's friends of friends.
answer: SELECT DISTINCT T4.name FROM PersonFriend AS T1 JOIN Person AS T2 ON T1.name  =  T2.name JOIN PersonFriend AS T3 ON T1.friend  =  T3.name JOIN PersonFriend AS T4 ON T3.friend  =  T4.name WHERE T2.name  =  'Alice' AND T4.name != 'Alice'

prefix_hints.hint_1: Treat `PersonFriend` as a directed relationship: `name` is the person and `friend` is that person's friend. Start with Alice's outgoing friendship rows and identify Alice by joining `T1.name = T2.name`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Follow the relationship a second time by joining another `PersonFriend` alias with `T1.friend = T3.name`; this makes `T3.friend` a friend of one of Alice's friends.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Join a final `PersonFriend` alias using `T3.friend = T4.name` so the resulting `T4.name` values correspond to people reached at the second friendship level.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Restrict the starting person with `T2.name = 'Alice'`, and exclude Alice from the result using `T4.name != 'Alice'`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the reached person's name from `T4.name` and apply `DISTINCT` so someone connected through multiple friendship paths appears only once.

metadata.question: Find Alice's friends of friends.

intermediate_turns.question: Can you please tell me who the friends of Alice's friends are?

Question:
List players' first name and last name who received salary from team Washington Nationals in both 2005 and 2007.
answer: SELECT T2.name_first ,  T2.name_last FROM salary AS T1 JOIN player AS T2 ON T1.player_id = T2.player_id JOIN team AS T3 ON T3.team_id_br = T1.team_id WHERE T1.year = 2005 AND T3.name = 'Washington Nationals' INTERSECT SELECT T2.name_first , T2.name_last FROM salary AS T1 JOIN player AS T2 ON T1.player_id = T2.player_id JOIN team AS T3 ON T3.team_id_br = T1.team_id WHERE T1.year = 2007 AND T3.name = 'Washington Nationals'

prefix_hints.hint_1: Build a result set for each requested year, since “both 2005 and 2007” requires players to qualify in two separate salary subsets.
prefix_hints.hint_2: For the 2005 subset, join `salary` to `player` using `salary.player_id = player.player_id` so each salary record can return the player’s name.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Connect each salary record to the team using the non-obvious identifier mapping `team.team_id_br = salary.team_id`, then filter with `salary.year = 2005` and `team.name = 'Washington Nationals'`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Construct an equivalent second SELECT with the same joins and team-name condition, changing the year filter to `salary.year = 2007`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project `name_first` and `name_last` in the same order from both SELECTs, and combine the two result sets with `INTERSECT` to retain players appearing in both years.

answer: SELECT T1.customer_name FROM customers AS T1 JOIN orders AS T2 JOIN order_items AS T3 JOIN products AS T4 ON T1.customer_id = T2.customer_id AND T2.order_id = T3.order_id AND T3.product_id = T4.product_id WHERE T4.product_name = "food" GROUP BY T1.customer_id HAVING count(*)  >=  1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Trace the purchase relationship from customers to their orders, then to order items, and finally to products.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Connect customers and orders with `Customers.customer_id = Orders.customer_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Extend the join chain using `Orders.order_id = Order_Items.order_id` and `Order_Items.product_id = Products.product_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Restrict the joined rows to the requested product with `WHERE Products.product_name = 'food'`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project each qualifying `customer_name`, grouping by `customer_id` and applying `HAVING COUNT(*) >= 1` so each customer is listed once after at least one matching purchase.

Question:
What are the name and id of the team offering the lowest average salary?
answer: SELECT T1.name ,  T1.team_id FROM team AS T1 JOIN salary AS T2 ON T1.team_id = T2.team_id GROUP BY T1.team_id ORDER BY avg(T2.salary) ASC LIMIT 1;

prefix_hints.hint_1: Use team records for the requested team name and ID, and salary records to measure what each team pays.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Connect the two sources through their shared identifier with `JOIN salary AS T2 ON T1.team_id = T2.team_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Group the joined salary rows by team using `GROUP BY T1.team_id` so `AVG(T2.salary)` is calculated separately for each team.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Sort the grouped teams by `AVG(T2.salary) ASC`, placing the team with the lowest average salary first.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Keep only the first sorted group with `LIMIT 1`, and project the team's `name` and `team_id`.

Question:
Find the name and price of the product that has been ordered the greatest number of times.
answer: SELECT t1.product_name ,   t1.product_price FROM products AS t1 JOIN regular_order_products AS t2 ON t1.product_id  =  t2.product_id GROUP BY t2.product_id ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Use the regular-order product association records to measure how many times each product has been ordered.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join product details to those order records using `Products.product_id = Regular_Order_Products.product_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Group the joined rows by `Regular_Order_Products.product_id` so that `COUNT(*)` represents the order frequency of each product.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Sort the groups by `COUNT(*) DESC` and apply `LIMIT 1` to retain the most frequently ordered product.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the winning product's `product_name` and `product_price` from `Products`.

answer: SELECT T1.customer_name FROM customers AS T1 JOIN customer_orders AS T2 ON T1.customer_id  =  T2.customer_id WHERE T1.payment_method_code  =  'Credit Card' GROUP BY T1.customer_id HAVING count(*)  >  2

prefix_hints.hint_2: Join the orders using `Customers.customer_id = Customer_Orders.customer_id` so each customer can be associated with all of their orders.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the joined rows to customers whose payment method is a credit card with `WHERE payment_method_code = 'Credit Card'`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Group the joined rows by `Customers.customer_id`, making each group represent one customer's orders, and apply `HAVING COUNT(*) > 2`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project `customer_name` from the grouped customer records to display the names that satisfy both conditions.

prefix_hints.hint_3: Filter this first joined set with `good_or_bad_customer = 'good'`.

prefix_hints.hint_5: Project `coupon_amount` in both SELECT branches so the intersection returns the amounts common to the qualifying good- and bad-customer coupon sets.

prefix_hints.hint_4: Join `PROFESSOR` to `DEPARTMENT` on `PROFESSOR.DEPT_CODE = DEPARTMENT.DEPT_CODE`, then filter with `DEPARTMENT.DEPT_NAME = 'Accounting'`.

Question:
What is the title and credits of the course that is taught in the largest classroom (with the highest capacity)?
answer: SELECT T3.title ,  T3.credits FROM classroom AS T1 JOIN SECTION AS T2 ON T1.building  =  T2.building AND T1.room_number  =  T2.room_number JOIN course AS T3 ON T2.course_id  =  T3.course_id WHERE T1.capacity  =  (SELECT max(capacity) FROM classroom)

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from classroom records because `capacity` determines which room is the largest, while the requested title and credits come from course data.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Relate each classroom to its scheduled sections using both room identifiers: `JOIN section ON classroom.building = section.building AND classroom.room_number = section.room_number`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Connect each matched section to its course with `section.course_id = course.course_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Identify the highest-capacity classroom with a scalar subquery, `(SELECT MAX(capacity) FROM classroom)`, and compare the joined classroom's capacity to that value in the `WHERE` clause.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the matched course's `title` and `credits`, preserving all courses taught in any classroom tied for the maximum capacity.

prefix_hints.hint_5: Combine the two station-ID result sets with `INTERSECT` so the output contains IDs satisfying both the San Francisco and average-availability conditions.

answer: SELECT title ,  film_id FROM film WHERE rental_rate  =  0.99 INTERSECT SELECT T1.title ,  T1.film_id FROM film AS T1 JOIN inventory AS T2 ON T1.film_id  =  T2.film_id GROUP BY T1.film_id HAVING count(*)  <  3

prefix_hints.hint_1: Build the first result set from `film`, selecting films whose `rental_rate` equals `0.99`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Build a second result set by joining `film` to `inventory` on their shared `film_id`, so each row represents an inventory copy of a film.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Group the joined rows by `T1.film_id` to calculate inventory totals separately for each film.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Keep films with fewer than three inventory records using `HAVING COUNT(*) < 3`, then combine this result with the fee-filtered set using `INTERSECT`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Ensure both sides of the set operation project matching columns in the same order: the film `title` followed by `film_id`.

Question:
Which customer, who has made at least one payment, has spent the least money? List his or her first name, last name, and the id.
answer: SELECT T1.first_name ,  T1.last_name ,  T1.customer_id FROM customer AS T1 JOIN payment AS T2 ON T1.customer_id  =  T2.customer_id GROUP BY T1.customer_id ORDER BY sum(amount) ASC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from customers who have payment records by joining `customer` to `payment` on their shared `customer_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Group the joined payment rows by `T1.customer_id` so each customer forms one result group.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Calculate each customer's total spending with `SUM(T2.amount)`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Sort the customer groups by that total in ascending order and use `LIMIT 1` to retain the smallest spender.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the selected customer's `first_name`, `last_name`, and `customer_id` from the customer table.
